cases.title: Status Asthmaticus
cases.stem: Ms. Asha Roy, a 29-year-old woman with severe asthma, arrives in the emergency department after using her rescue inhaler repeatedly without relief. She is sitting upright, speaking only one or two words at a time, and appears frightened. She has marked accessory muscle use and audible wheeze. Her vital signs are blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, pulse 132 beats per minute, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 88% on room air, and peak expiratory flow is critically reduced. The nurse knows this may represent status asthmaticus. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Asthmaticus | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which cues indicate severe asthma exacerbation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Accessory muscle use
Unable to speak full sentences
Repeated rescue inhaler use without relief
Tachycardia
Oxygen saturation 88%

questions.rationale: All findings are signs of severe asthma and impending respiratory failure risk. Repeated ineffective use of a rescue inhaler indicates poor response to home therapy. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Asthmaticus | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Status asthmaticus or severe uncontrolled asthma requiring urgent intervention
Panic attack without airway obstruction
Mild asthma that can wait
Stable chronic cough only

questions.rationale: This is an emergency presentation. The inability to speak normally, low oxygen saturation, and high work of breathing signal severe bronchospasm and possible respiratory exhaustion. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Asthmaticus | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Ineffective airway clearance and impaired ventilation due to severe bronchospasm
Knowledge deficit about long-term exercise
Fear of hospitalisation
Risk for constipation

questions.rationale: The immediate danger is ventilation failure due to severe airway narrowing. Fear is secondary to the respiratory emergency. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Asthmaticus | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay treatment until a full medication history is completed
Support oxygenation, initiate emergency asthma management, and monitor closely for worsening fatigue or silent chest
Offer food and ask the patient to lie flat
Instruct the patient to take slower breaths without treatment

questions.rationale: Severe asthma requires immediate emergency management. A silent chest or increasing fatigue may indicate impending respiratory failure. Lying flat, delaying treatment, or providing only verbal coaching would be unsafe. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Asthmaticus | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Calm, focused reassurance during treatment
Assuming wheeze always means the airway is improving
Continuous reassessment of breath sounds and oxygenation
Monitoring for exhaustion and reduced air movement
Preparing for escalation if the patient stops responding to therapy

questions.rationale: Reassessment and escalation planning are essential. Wheeze does not automatically mean improvement; diminishing wheeze with worsening distress can signal critically reduced airflow. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Asthmaticus | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that treatment is helping?

options.text: Oxygenation stays poor and fatigue worsens
Air movement decreases further and the patient becomes drowsy
The patient can speak more comfortably, oxygen saturation improves, and work of breathing decreases
The nurse stops reassessing once the first nebuliser is complete

questions.rationale: Improvement in speech, oxygenation, and effort of breathing suggests better ventilation and reduced bronchospasm.

cases.title: Ischemic Stroke in the Treatment Window
cases.stem: Mrs. Helen George, a 67-year-old woman, is brought to the emergency department after her husband noticed sudden left-sided facial droop, slurred speech, and weakness in the left arm 45 minutes ago. She is awake but frightened and unable to answer fully. Her husband confirms that she was normal at breakfast and the symptoms began abruptly. Blood pressure is 178/96 mmHg, pulse 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and glucose is normal. The nurse must act rapidly because time-sensitive stroke interventions may still be possible. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Ischemic Stroke in the Treatment Window | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings are classic acute stroke cues? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sudden facial droop
Fear and confusion
Slurred speech
Unilateral arm weakness
Abrupt onset 45 minutes ago

questions.rationale: The major neurological cues are facial droop, dysarthria, and unilateral weakness. The precise time of onset is critically important because it affects eligibility for reperfusion therapies. Fear and confusion may accompany the event and should also be acknowledged. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Ischemic Stroke in the Treatment Window | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Mild anxiety attack
Migraine with no urgency
Chronic dementia only
Likely acute ischemic stroke requiring urgent stroke pathway activation

questions.rationale: The presentation strongly suggests acute stroke. The abrupt onset and focal deficits are classic. NCLEX questions in stroke management emphasise speed, onset time, and prioritised imaging and assessment. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Ischemic Stroke in the Treatment Window | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed sleep
Risk for constipation
Acute neurological perfusion problem with risk of irreversible brain injury
Knowledge deficit about diet

questions.rationale: The most urgent problem is acute interruption of cerebral perfusion. Brain tissue is time-sensitive, so rapid action is required. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Ischemic Stroke in the Treatment Window | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay action until family finishes talking
Ask the patient to walk to show strength
Encourage the patient to drink water to relax
Activate the stroke pathway, maintain safety, and prepare for urgent imaging and neurological assessment

questions.rationale: Time is critical in stroke care. Immediate pathway activation, safety, and preparation for imaging take priority. Oral intake should not be offered until swallowing is assessed. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Ischemic Stroke in the Treatment Window | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume all strokes are haemorrhagic without imaging
Document the exact last-known-well time
Monitor airway, blood pressure, and neurological changes closely
Keep the patient NPO until swallow safety is determined
Provide calm explanations to patient and family

questions.rationale: Last-known-well time is essential for treatment planning. Airway and neuro reassessment are priorities. NPO status protects against aspiration. Imaging is required to distinguish stroke type; assumptions without imaging are unsafe. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Ischemic Stroke in the Treatment Window | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that the immediate nursing management has been effective while definitive therapy is organised?

options.text: The nurse stops monitoring because imaging is pending
The patient remains safe, neurological status is closely monitored, aspiration risk is prevented, and the stroke team is fully engaged
Blood pressure worsens with no reassessment
The patient is given food before swallow assessment

questions.rationale: In the early phase, effective nursing management is shown by safety, rapid pathway activation, and prevention of secondary complications rather than instant symptom resolution.

cases.title: Increased Intracranial Pressure after Head Injury
cases.stem: Mr. Sean Mathew, a 35-year-old man, is admitted after a motor vehicle collision with a moderate traumatic brain injury. During the first hours on the ward he was awake but drowsy. Over the next hour, the nurse notices that he becomes harder to arouse and begins vomiting. His speech is slower and less organised than before. Vital signs now show blood pressure 168/70 mmHg, pulse 54 beats per minute, respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute, and intermittent unequal pupil response. The nurse recognises possible rising intracranial pressure. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Increased Intracranial Pressure after Head Injury | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings support increased intracranial pressure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Widened pulse pressure pattern
Bradycardia
Pupil changes
Worsening level of consciousness
Vomiting

questions.rationale: These are all concerning findings. Worsening LOC is often an early warning sign. Vomiting, bradycardia, abnormal blood pressure pattern, and pupil changes fit rising ICP and possible neurological deterioration. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Increased Intracranial Pressure after Head Injury | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The patient may be developing increased intracranial pressure requiring urgent intervention
Benign headache with no urgency
Mild dehydration only
The patient is simply sleepy from rest needs

questions.rationale: The trend is dangerous and compatible with increasing ICP. The nurse must respond urgently because neurological decline can become irreversible. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Increased Intracranial Pressure after Head Injury | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for impaired cerebral perfusion and brain herniation
Need for menu change
Knowledge deficit
Disturbed sleep

questions.rationale: The greatest danger is loss of cerebral perfusion and possible herniation. This is a neurological emergency. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Increased Intracranial Pressure after Head Injury | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the patient to get up and walk
Delay action until routine review
Provide a large meal
Elevate the head as appropriate, maintain airway and oxygenation, minimise stimulation, and urgently escalate neurological deterioration

questions.rationale: Head elevation, airway protection, reduced stimulation, and urgent escalation are key priorities. Ambulation, feeding, or waiting would be unsafe. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Increased Intracranial Pressure after Head Injury | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitoring for worsening respiratory pattern
Frequent neuro checks and pupil assessment
Ignoring vomiting if blood pressure seems acceptable
Preparing for urgent imaging or critical care intervention as ordered
Avoiding unnecessary coughing or straining where possible

questions.rationale: Close neurological monitoring, respiratory assessment, avoidance of actions that may raise ICP, and preparation for higher-level intervention are all appropriate. Vomiting should never be ignored in this context. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Increased Intracranial Pressure after Head Injury | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improved stability?

options.text: The nurse stops neuro checks after one assessment
Level of consciousness stabilises, pupils remain more consistent, and vital signs move away from the dangerous pattern
Bradycardia worsens with slower respirations
The patient becomes more unresponsive and vomiting continues

questions.rationale: Improvement is demonstrated by neurological stabilisation and less concerning vital sign patterns.

cases.title: Status Epilepticus
cases.stem: Ms. Priyanka Nair, a 41-year-old patient with a history of seizure disorder, is brought to the emergency department actively seizing. According to her family, the seizure started more than five minutes ago and she has not regained consciousness. They say she may have missed her medication for two days due to vomiting. The nurse observes ongoing tonic-clonic movements, cyanosis around the lips, and copious oral secretions. Vital signs are difficult to obtain immediately, but oxygen saturation is falling and the patient is at risk of airway compromise. The nurse must act rapidly. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Epilepticus | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which features make this a high-risk seizure emergency? Select all that apply.

options.text: No return to consciousness
Ongoing seizure beyond five minutes
Missed medication history
Falling oxygenation
Cyanosis and secretions

questions.rationale: These findings indicate status epilepticus and immediate risk to airway, breathing, and neurological function. Duration over five minutes and lack of recovery are especially significant. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Epilepticus | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Brief uncomplicated seizure
Stable postictal rest state
Mild anxiety episode
Status epilepticus requiring emergency airway and medication management

questions.rationale: The patient is not in a benign postictal period. Continuous seizure activity without recovery is a medical emergency. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Epilepticus | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Airway compromise and hypoxia during prolonged seizure activity
Risk for constipation
Need for discharge planning
Disturbed body image

questions.rationale: Airway and oxygenation must come first. Prolonged seizure activity also risks brain injury, but the nurse addresses this through airway safety and urgent medication support. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Epilepticus | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Protect the airway and patient safety, provide oxygen support, and prepare for emergency seizure management
Leave the patient alone until the seizure stops
Restrain the limbs tightly
Force an oral object into the mouth

questions.rationale: The nurse should focus on airway, oxygenation, and protection from injury. Objects must never be forced into the mouth, and tight restraint can cause harm. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Epilepticus | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Suction secretions as needed and safe
Time the seizure and document events
Assume missing medication is unimportant
Prepare for IV access and emergency anticonvulsant therapy
Turn the patient away from injury when feasible

questions.rationale: Timing, medication preparation, secretion management, and protection from injury are correct. The missed medication history is clinically relevant and should not be dismissed. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Status Epilepticus | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that immediate care has been effective?

options.text: The nurse leaves after the seizure ends
Seizure activity stops, oxygenation improves, airway is maintained, and the patient begins postictal recovery under close observation
Secretions obstruct the airway without intervention
Cyanosis worsens and no reassessment occurs

questions.rationale: Successful immediate management ends seizure activity, improves oxygenation, and maintains safe observation during recovery.

cases.title: Acute Kidney Injury with Hyperkalaemia
cases.stem: Mrs. Noreen D’Silva, a 68-year-old patient with sepsis and reduced urine output, develops worsening weakness and palpitations. She has had only 15 mL urine output in the last hour, and the latest lab results show potassium 6.5 mmol/L and rising creatinine. The telemetry monitor shows concerning rhythm changes. She looks fatigued and says her legs feel heavy. Blood pressure is 100/64 mmHg, pulse 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and skin is cool. The nurse recognises combined renal compromise and dangerous electrolyte imbalance. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Acute Kidney Injury with Hyperkalaemia | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings indicate urgent hyperkalaemia with renal dysfunction? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rising creatinine and oliguria
Palpitations and rhythm changes
Heavy legs
Weakness
Potassium 6.5 mmol/L

questions.rationale: All findings support severe hyperkalaemia in the setting of acute kidney injury. Rhythm changes are especially dangerous because they may precede cardiac arrest. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Acute Kidney Injury with Hyperkalaemia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Acute kidney injury with life-threatening hyperkalaemia requiring emergency management
Stable kidney disease only
Benign muscle fatigue
Mild dehydration alone

questions.rationale: The patient’s oliguria, rising creatinine, and high potassium indicate a renal emergency with cardiac implications. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Acute Kidney Injury with Hyperkalaemia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Knowledge deficit about food
Risk for loneliness
Risk for lethal dysrhythmia related to hyperkalaemia
Disturbed sleep

questions.rationale: The cardiac effects of hyperkalaemia take priority because they may rapidly become fatal. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Acute Kidney Injury with Hyperkalaemia | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay action until the next lab draw
Encourage a potassium-rich snack
Ensure continuous monitoring, escalate urgently, and prepare for immediate hyperkalaemia treatment as prescribed
Send the patient walking to the bathroom

questions.rationale: Continuous monitoring and urgent treatment preparation are critical. Any delay increases the risk of cardiac arrest. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Acute Kidney Injury with Hyperkalaemia | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Track urine output carefully
Ignore weakness if the monitor alarm is quiet for a moment
Anticipate repeat potassium measurement after treatment
Recheck rhythm and mental status frequently
Review medications that may worsen potassium retention

questions.rationale: The nurse must reassess continuously, review contributing factors, trend potassium, and monitor kidney output. Weakness remains clinically relevant and should not be ignored. Program Area: Advanced Adult Nursing Care II | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Acute Kidney Injury with Hyperkalaemia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Potassium trends downward, rhythm stabilises, and symptoms lessen
The nurse stops monitoring after one treatment
Palpitations become stronger
Oliguria worsens with increasing ECG instability

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by falling potassium, improved rhythm stability, and reduced symptoms.
